newsitem.title: UK: Yugoslav move on IMF helps, a little - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav move on IMF helps, a little - bankers.

text.p: Yugoslavia's attempt to win over the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is a help but unlikely to be enough by itself to bring in urgently-needed foreign capital soon, bankers and traders said on Monday.
Yugoslav parliament last week approved what the government says are all the conditions set by the IMF to restore Belgrade's membership.

"IMF membership does make a difference. I can't see them getting any commercial finance until they've got membership. But it's only the very first step," said one trader, actively involved in trading the commercial debt of former Yugoslavia.

Belgrade, its economy in tatters after years of sanctions over the Bosnian war, is trying to negotiate a deal with banks on the about $2 billion of foreign commercial debt it inherited after the collapse of the old Yugoslav federation.
An agreement with the commercial banks is crucial if Belgrade wants to tap the international market again for funds.

Two republics, Croatia and Slovenia, have already signed deals with banks on their portion of the debt, though Belgrade -- which they have excluded from any repayments -- has lodged, or threatend to lodge, lawsuits to unravel both agreements.
Smaller amounts are also still owed by Macedonia and Bosnia.
One banker said an agreement with the IMF was less vital than trying to resolve how to share out the assets left behind when the country split apart five years ago.
"They have got to sort out these assets. It wouldn't make sense to strike a deal with banks without that," he said.
He estimated Serbia's foreign exchanges reserves were probably no more than $400 million.
Yugoslav officials are due to hold technical talks with banks about the middle of this month and full negotiations in October.
Creditor sources said scant progress was made in talks in July.
"It was a little bit disappointing," one said, adding Yugoslav officials had not come up with any substantial proposals to settle the debts.
"Joining the IMF is good but it's not the breakthrough we want. That will be when they propose a deal structure. I have a sense things have drifted a bit," another banker said.
Even it does join the IMF, there are still large questionmarks over whether the authorities will want to institute reforms needed before the IMF would be prepared to lend any money.
